title: Clone a repository and understand what you actually got
summary: A clone is not a download of the latest files. It is a full copy of the object database plus one checked-out branch. Prove it by finding history the clone never asked for.
mental_model: Clone copies every commit, tree and blob the server has, then checks out one branch. Everything else is still there — you just have to ask for it by name. That is why git works on a plane.

steps.title: Look at what the clone knows
steps.why: Switch the terminal dropdown on the right to `teammate` — that is the clone. It has the full log even though you never fetched anything after cloning.
steps.expect: Two commits and an origin pointing at a path ending in origin.git.

steps.title: Find the branch you did not check out
steps.why: `git branch` shows only local branches — there is exactly one. `-a` reveals the remote-tracking branches, which are read-only bookmarks of what the server had at clone time.
steps.expect: One local branch, plus remotes/origin/main and remotes/origin/release/1.0.

steps.title: The release branch was in the clone all along
steps.why: The commit exists locally already. Creating a local branch from it needs no network at all — proof that clone copied the whole object database, not just the checked-out files.

verify.label: you are on a local release/1.0

steps.title: See the tracking relationship git set up for you
steps.why: Because the branch was created from `origin/release/1.0`, git recorded an upstream. That is what lets you type a bare `git push` or `git pull` later without naming anything.

steps.title: Look at the server side
steps.why: origin.git is a bare repository: all the git data, no working tree. That is what every server-side repo is — GitHub is a bare repo with a website bolted on.
steps.expect: core.bare = true, and directories like objects/ and refs/ instead of your files.

verify.label: the clone has a local release/1.0 checked out
verify.hint: git switch -c release/1.0 origin/release/1.0 (run it in the teammate clone)

verify.label: it tracks origin
verify.hint: create it from origin/release/1.0 so git records the upstream automatically

verify.label: the release file is in the clone's working tree
the server repo is bare, as every server repo is

pitfalls: `git clone --depth 1` gives a shallow clone: fast, but `git log` and `git bisect` are crippled until you `--unshallow`.
Remote-tracking branches like `origin/main` do not update by themselves. They move only when you fetch or pull.
You cannot commit on `origin/main` — it is a bookmark, not a branch. Checking it out gives you a detached HEAD.
cheatsheet: full copy of the object database plus one checked-out branch
clone into a directory of your choosing
local branch from a remote one, with tracking set up
each branch, its upstream and its ahead/behind counts
the server-shaped copy: no working tree
